one_liner: 3-prime NTT big-integer multiply (AVX2 CPU, CUDA GPU) inside a Windows hobby language; beats single-core GMP only on GPU or decimal I/O.
what_it_does: TzdLang is a new scripting language (bytecode VM, LLVM ORC JIT, LibTorch bindings) whose interpreter multiplies multi-million-digit integers with its own number-theoretic-transform engines. The CPU engine (Generated/TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp, enabled with --experimental-compute) exposes bigint_mul_experimental_cpu_str(a, b) on decimal strings and bigint_mul_experimental_cpu_limbs on base-10^9 limb vectors; the GPU engine lives in Generated/TzdPyTorch.cpp and is selected with --forceGPU. There is no standalone library, header or API outside the interpreter: reusing it means copying source files.
how_it_is_fast: Numbers are stored as base-10^9 limbs, so parsing and printing decimal strings is linear chunking instead of GMP's binary/decimal radix conversion, which is where most of the 14.5x/45.1x end-to-end gains come from. The product is a cyclic convolution done as three 32-bit NTTs (primes 998244353, 985661441, 754974721 in the current source) with AVX2 Montgomery multiplication, Bailey's four-step decomposition into cache-sized row transforms with tiled transposes, OpenMP threads, and Garner CRT reconstruction. The GPU engine runs the same scheme as NVRTC-compiled Stockham kernels with shared-memory padding and a parallel carry scan.
when_to_use: As reference code for a 3-prime 32-bit NTT multiplier with AVX2 Montgomery arithmetic and four-step cache blocking.

Workloads that start and end as decimal strings of millions of digits (e.g. printing huge products), where avoiding binary/decimal conversion dominates: the wiki's end-to-end run is 175 ms CPU and 57 ms GPU vs 2,549 ms for single-core GMP at 4.74M digits.

Windows x64 machines with an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 6.0+ when one multiplication of roughly 1M-38M digits must finish faster than single-core GMP (GPU kernel 29.2 ms vs 111.8 ms at 4.74M digits; complete GPU product 42.0 ms).
when_not_to_use: As a faster CPU multiplier than GMP: the complete CPU product (54.02 ms NTT + 97.08 ms CRT/carry = 151.1 ms on 8 threads) is slower than single-threaded GMP mpz_mul (111.78 ms) on the same i7-4790.

Any project that needs a library: the code is embedded in an interpreter that also pulls in ANTLR-generated sources, LLVM, LibTorch and CUDA, and the repository has no LICENSE file (MIT appears only in the README and badge).
Linux, macOS or non-AVX2 CPUs: the CPU engine uses AVX2 intrinsics unconditionally and the MSVC _umul128 intrinsic, and the README lists Windows 10/11 x64 with Visual Studio as the platform.

Very large operands on the CPU path: nothing checks the 2^22-element transform limit (P2 = 235*2^22+1), so combined inputs above about 4.19M limbs (~37.7M digits) would compute with an invalid root of unity; the GPU path throws instead.
Anything beyond multiplication of non-negative decimal strings with a sign: no division, modular arithmetic or binary-limb interface is exposed by this engine.

integration.form: source-drop (two files inside an interpreter; no library target)
integration.dependencies: CPU engine: OpenMP, AVX2, MSVC intrinsics (_umul128); GPU engine: CUDA Toolkit 12+ with NVRTC, LibTorch (used to detect CUDA), compute capability 6.0+; the full build also wants LLVM and ANTLR4
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (CMakeLists.txt), Visual Studio 2022/2026 (MSVC v143/v145) or CMake 3.20+
integration.platforms: Windows 10/11 x64 only per README; AVX2 required for the CPU engine; NVIDIA Pascal or newer for the GPU engine
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the CPU engine's global twiddle cache checks its size outside the mutex and sets the new size before the tables are built, so concurrent multiplications of different sizes can race

gotchas: The headline CPU '2.07x faster than GMP' times only the NTT phase; the --bigTime breakdown shows a 97.08 ms serial CRT/carry step that is excluded, and the GMP side is a complete mpz_mul.

The wiki and the code disagree: the wiki lists primes 469762049/167772161/754974721, a Kogge-Stone carry chain and a fast_div_1e9 helper for the CPU path, while TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp uses 998244353/985661441/754974721, a sequential carry loop and plain division. The wiki's fast_div_1e9 snippet also returns a wrong quotient for some inputs above about 1.23e19 (checked by script), though the current code does not call it.

README and wiki give two different multi-threaded GMP end-to-end figures (~519 ms and 2,522.09 ms), and the 'multi-threaded GMP' rows are the author's own Karatsuba split over mpz_mul, not a GMP feature; all figures are single runs.

GPU timings are taken after a warm-up multiplication at the same size with cached device buffers and twiddles (the sample output shows alloc=0.00 ms, twiddle=0.00 ms), and the kernels are NVRTC-compiled with --use_fast_math.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick FLINT or mp++ for a maintained library that beats GMP on large multiplications with full arithmetic, and CGBN or the GMP-on-GPU entries for batched fixed-size GPU work; TzdLanguage is only worth opening as readable NTT/CRT example code or if your inputs and outputs are huge decimal strings on a Windows/CUDA box.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README/wiki figures for one 4,741,006-digit multiplication on an Intel Core i7-4790 (4C/8T) and an NVIDIA P106-090: GPU NTT kernel 29.20 ms (42.01 ms with CRT, carry and copy) and CPU AVX2 NTT 54.02 ms (151.1 ms with CRT/carry) vs single-core GMP 6.3.0 mpz_mul 111.78 ms from a vcpkg MSVC build (cl /O2 /openmp), so only the GPU path beats GMP on the multiply itself (about 2.66x, derived from page data); end-to-end decimal-string-to-string times are 56.52 ms GPU and 175.41 ms CPU vs 2,549.30 ms for GMP.
status_note: Very young (first commit 2026-09-13, 81 commits, 10 stars, last commit 2026-09-30) and changing daily; no LICENSE file was present on 2026-10-01 (raw LICENSE 404) despite the README's MIT claim, so copying the code carries licence risk until one is added.
